items.title: Dollar General’s price lawsuit expands to 30 states
items.summary: Ten more states joined a federal lawsuit over alleged gaps between advertised prices and what shoppers paid at checkout. Here’s how to document a mismatch.
paragraphs: The Federal Trade Commission filed an amended complaint on November 20, adding Delaware, Georgia, Kentucky, Maine, Minnesota, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina and South Dakota. The FTC and the original 20 states filed the case on October 26 in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee.

The complaint alleges that Dollar General repeatedly charged more at checkout than prices displayed on shelves, tags or in advertisements. Oregon’s attorney general says the suit asks the court to order pricing changes, penalties and money back for overcharged shoppers. Those are requests, not a court finding or a refund program. The case is pending, and the November 20 announcement did not open a claim process or establish a refund deadline.

In its October 26 response to the original lawsuit, Dollar General said discrepancies can happen despite its pricing procedures, that store teams are expected to address them, and that it disputes how the FTC calculated potential refunds and will defend the case.
items.takeaway: If a price looks wrong, save the itemized receipt and, if you can, photograph the shelf tag with the product size and any sale terms visible. Ask the store to review the mismatch. If it’s unresolved, your state consumer protection office can take a complaint. Filing a complaint is not a refund claim.
items.status_note: Pending lawsuit. No refund claim process announced.

items.title: Budgeting for Medicare? The 2027 Part B premium is $209.40
items.summary: The standard monthly premium rises $6.50 in January. December 7 is the deadline for most Medicare open-enrollment plan changes.
paragraphs: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced on November 17 that the standard Medicare Part B premium will be $209.40 a month in 2027, up from $202.90 in 2026. The annual Part B deductible rises to $292 from $283. The standard premium isn’t what every person pays: some pay an income-related adjustment, and assistance may help eligible people with costs.

Medicare’s annual open enrollment runs through December 7. The plan must receive an enrollment request by that date; changes made during that window take effect January 1, 2027. The standard Part B amount is separate from any premium a Medicare Advantage or drug plan charges. Changing plans is not required simply because the standard amount increased.
items.takeaway: Before deciding whether to keep or change coverage, compare your plan’s 2027 premiums, other out-of-pocket costs, drug coverage and participating providers. If you’re considering a change, confirm timing with Medicare or the plan.

items.body_markdown:
The standard monthly premium rises $6.50 in January. December 7 is the deadline for most Medicare open-enrollment plan changes.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced on November 17 that the standard Medicare Part B premium will be $209.40 a month in 2027, up from $202.90 in 2026. The annual Part B deductible rises to $292 from $283. The standard premium isn’t what every person pays: some pay an income-related adjustment, and assistance may help eligible people with costs.

Medicare’s annual open enrollment runs through December 7. The plan must receive an enrollment request by that date; changes made during that window take effect January 1, 2027. The standard Part B amount is separate from any premium a Medicare Advantage or drug plan charges. Changing plans is not required simply because the standard amount increased.

What you can do: Before deciding whether to keep or change coverage, compare your plan’s 2027 premiums, other out-of-pocket costs, drug coverage and participating providers. If you’re considering a change, confirm timing with Medicare or the plan.
